Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery

Author

Cao Jinming

Published

May 24, 2026

Modified

May 9, 2026

Academic-use note. This is a working technical-report draft and reproducible analysis scaffold. Before submission, review the charts, refine the wording in your own voice, and keep only findings you can explain.

1 Overview

This report applies visual analytics to a real-world Spanish motor insurance portfolio dataset from Mendeley Data. The portfolio contains policy-level transactions from 2022 to 2024, including policy attributes, premium components, claim counts, incurred losses, and exposure.

The analysis addresses two required tasks:

  1. Univariate visual analytics: explore the distributions and characteristics of numerical and categorical variables.
  2. Bivariate visual analytics: investigate and statistically validate factors associated with portfolio profitability and volatility.

For this report:

  • Profitability is represented by profit = total_premium - total_incurred and the aggregate loss ratio total_incurred / total_premium.
  • Volatility is represented by the spread and upper tail of individual policy loss ratios, claim occurrence, and high-incurred outliers.

2 Analytical sandbox

2.1 Packages and helper functions

library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)
library(scales)
library(patchwork)
library(knitr)
if (file.exists("TH_Ex/th_ex1_common.R")) {
  source("TH_Ex/th_ex1_common.R")
} else {
  source("th_ex1_common.R")
}

2.3 Derived analytical variables

The key derived variables are created in TH_Ex/th_ex1_common.R:

  • profit = total_premium - total_incurred
  • loss_ratio = total_incurred / total_premium
  • loss_ratio_cap: loss ratio capped at the 99th percentile for robust visual comparison
  • claim_flag = total_claims > 0
  • claim_frequency = total_claims / total_exposure
  • severity = total_incurred / total_claims, only for claim records
  • driver_age_band and vehicle_age_band for segment-level comparison
portfolio_size <- tibble(
  measure = c("Records", "Distinct insured IDs", "Years", "Variables after derivation"),
  value = c(nrow(motor), n_distinct(motor$insured_id), paste(levels(motor$year), collapse = ", "), ncol(motor))
)

kable(portfolio_size)
measure value

2.4 Data quality checks

missing_tbl <- motor |>
  summarise(across(everything(), ~sum(is.na(.x)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "missing_records") |>
  filter(missing_records > 0) |>
  arrange(desc(missing_records))

kable(missing_tbl)
variable missing_records
severity 303333
fuel_type 1287
vehicle_value 513
loss_ratio 49
claim_frequency 49
vehicle_age 2
age_driving_licence 2
vehicle_age_band 2

Draft interpretation to customise: Missingness is limited for core profitability fields. The largest missing count is expected for severity because severity is only meaningful when at least one claim occurred. A small amount of missingness appears in vehicle-related fields and should be noted, but it is unlikely to dominate portfolio-level results.

3 Task 1: Univariate visual analytics

3.1 Numerical variables

num_profile <- motor |>
  summarise(across(
    c(driver_age, vehicle_age, age_driving_licence, vehicle_value, power_to_weight_ratio,
      total_premium, total_claims, total_incurred, total_exposure, profit, loss_ratio),
    list(
      min = ~min(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
      q25 = ~quantile(.x, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
      median = ~median(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
      mean = ~mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
      q75 = ~quantile(.x, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
      max = ~max(.x, na.rm = TRUE)
    ),
    .names = "{.col}_{.fn}"
  )) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = c("variable", ".value"), names_pattern = "(.+)_(min|q25|median|mean|q75|max)")

motor |>
  select(driver_age, vehicle_age, vehicle_value, total_premium, total_incurred, loss_ratio_cap) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, colour = "white", fill = "#2c7fb8") +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free", ncol = 3) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of selected numerical variables",
    subtitle = "Loss ratio is capped at the 99th percentile for readability.",
    x = NULL, y = "Number of records"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Draft interpretation to customise: The portfolio has many zero-claim records, so incurred losses and loss ratios are highly right-skewed. Premiums and vehicle values are also skewed, but less extremely than incurred losses. This means median and percentile summaries are more informative than means alone.

3.2 Categorical variables

cat_vars <- c("policy_type", "policy_status", "business_type", "payment_frequency", "bonus_score", "fuel_type", "municipality_type", "circulation_area")

motor |>
  select(all_of(cat_vars)) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "category") |>
  mutate(category = fct_explicit_na(as.factor(category), na_level = "Missing")) |>
  count(variable, category) |>
  group_by(variable) |>
  mutate(pct = n / sum(n), category = fct_reorder(category, pct)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  ggplot(aes(x = category, y = pct)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#41ab5d") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = pct) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of selected categorical variables",
    x = NULL, y = "Share of records"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Draft interpretation to customise: CC and COMP_E dominate the coverage mix. The portfolio is also strongly concentrated in annual payment frequency and good bonus score. This concentration matters because small categories can have unstable loss-ratio estimates even when they appear extreme.

4 Task 2: Bivariate visual analytics and validation

4.1 Portfolio trend by year

yearly <- portfolio_summary(motor, year)
kable(yearly, digits = 3)

yearly |>
  select(year, premium, incurred, profit) |>
  pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "measure", values_to = "amount") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = amount, colour = measure, group = measure)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = money) +
  labs(
    title = "Premium, incurred loss, and profit by year",

  ) +
  theme_minimal()
yearly |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = loss_ratio, group = 1)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "#d95f0e") +
  geom_point(size = 3, colour = "#d95f0e") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = pct) +
  labs(
    title = "Aggregate loss ratio increased in 2024",
    x = NULL, y = "Loss ratio"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Draft interpretation to customise: Premium volume and incurred losses both increase over time, but the aggregate loss ratio rises most clearly in 2024. This suggests that growth in premium did not fully offset growth in incurred losses.

  geom_boxplot(fill = "#9ecae1", outlier.alpha = 0.08) +

Draft interpretation to customise: Comprehensive products have higher aggregate loss ratios than third-party products, especially COMP_N. The boxplot shows that much of the risk comes from a long right tail rather than from the typical policy record.

4.3 Bonus score, fuel type, and circulation area

seg_long <- bind_rows(
  portfolio_summary(motor, bonus_score) |> mutate(segment = "bonus_score", category = as.character(bonus_score)),
  portfolio_summary(motor, fuel_type) |> mutate(segment = "fuel_type", category = fct_explicit_na(as.factor(fuel_type), "Missing") |> as.character()),
  portfolio_summary(motor, circulation_area) |> mutate(segment = "circulation_area", category = as.character(circulation_area))
)

seg_long |>
  mutate(category = fct_reorder(category, loss_ratio)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = category, y = loss_ratio)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#756bb1") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = pct) +
  facet_wrap(~ segment, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    title = "Loss ratio differs across risk-related categories",
    x = NULL, y = "Aggregate loss ratio"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Draft interpretation to customise: Non-good bonus scores, diesel vehicles, and urban circulation show higher loss ratios in this portfolio. These differences should be interpreted with business context because category mix and exposure size differ.

4.4 Age segments

age_driver <- portfolio_summary(motor, driver_age_band) |> mutate(segment = "Driver age", category = as.character(driver_age_band))
age_vehicle <- portfolio_summary(motor, vehicle_age_band) |> mutate(segment = "Vehicle age", category = as.character(vehicle_age_band))

bind_rows(age_driver, age_vehicle) |>
  filter(!is.na(category)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = category, y = loss_ratio, group = segment, colour = segment)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = pct) +
  facet_wrap(~ segment, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(
    title = "Loss ratio by driver-age and vehicle-age bands",
    x = NULL, y = "Aggregate loss ratio"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Draft interpretation to customise: Loss ratio is not monotonic by age. Mid-age drivers and very old drivers show elevated aggregate ratios, while vehicle-age bands from 4 to 20 years appear less favourable than the oldest vehicle band. This indicates that underwriting interpretation should account for product mix and exposure, not age alone.

4.5 Brand-level volatility screen

brand_tbl <- motor |>
  group_by(vehicle_brand) |>
  summarise(
    records = n(),
    exposure = sum(total_exposure, na.rm = TRUE),
    premium = sum(total_premium, na.rm = TRUE),
    incurred = sum(total_incurred, na.rm = TRUE),
    claims = sum(total_claims, na.rm = TRUE),
    loss_ratio = incurred / premium,
    claim_frequency = claims / exposure,
    p95_loss_ratio = quantile(loss_ratio, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  filter(exposure >= 1000)

brand_tbl |>
  ggplot(aes(x = claim_frequency, y = loss_ratio, size = exposure)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.65, colour = "#08519c") +
  geom_text(
    data = brand_tbl |> slice_max(loss_ratio, n = 8),
    aes(label = vehicle_brand), vjust = -0.8, size = 3, check_overlap = TRUE
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = number_format(accuracy = 0.01)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = pct) +
  scale_size_continuous(labels = comma) +
  labs(
    title = "Brand-level screen for high loss ratio and claim frequency",
    subtitle = "Only brands with exposure >= 1,000 are shown.",
    x = "Claim frequency", y = "Aggregate loss ratio", size = "Exposure"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Draft interpretation to customise: This chart is a screening device rather than a final underwriting decision. Brands in the upper-right area combine higher claim frequency and higher loss ratio, making them candidates for deeper investigation.

4.6 Statistical validation

Because individual loss ratio is highly skewed and zero-inflated, non-parametric tests are used for group differences. The Kruskal-Wallis test is applied to the 99th-percentile-capped loss ratio. Chi-square tests are used to validate whether claim occurrence differs by segment.

test_vars <- c("policy_type", "bonus_score", "driver_age_band", "vehicle_age_band", "fuel_type", "circulation_area", "year")

kw_tbl <- map_dfr(test_vars, \(v) {
  kt <- kruskal.test(as.formula(paste("loss_ratio_cap ~", v)), data = motor)
  tibble(test = "Kruskal-Wallis", variable = v, statistic = unname(kt$statistic), p_value = kt$p.value)
})

chi_tbl <- map_dfr(test_vars, \(v) {
  ct <- chisq.test(table(motor[[v]], motor$claim_flag))
  tibble(test = "Chi-square", variable = v, statistic = unname(ct$statistic), p_value = ct$p.value)
})

validation_tbl <- bind_rows(kw_tbl, chi_tbl) |>
  mutate(p_value_label = format.pval(p_value, digits = 3)) |>
  select(test, variable, statistic, p_value_label)

kable(validation_tbl, digits = 2)
test variable statistic p_value_label
Kruskal-Wallis policy_type 7287.56 <2e-16
Kruskal-Wallis bonus_score 286.90 <2e-16
Kruskal-Wallis driver_age_band 266.94 <2e-16
Kruskal-Wallis vehicle_age_band 303.78 <2e-16
Kruskal-Wallis fuel_type 800.33 <2e-16

Chi-square policy_type 6638.42 <2e-16

corr_tbl <- map_dfr(
  c("driver_age", "vehicle_age", "age_driving_licence", "vehicle_value", "seats", "power_to_weight_ratio", "total_premium"),
  \(v) {
    ct <- suppressWarnings(cor.test(motor[[v]], motor$loss_ratio_cap, method = "spearman", exact = FALSE))
    tibble(variable = v, spearman_rho = unname(ct$estimate), p_value = ct$p.value)
  }
) |>
  mutate(p_value_label = format.pval(p_value, digits = 3)) |>
  arrange(desc(abs(spearman_rho)))

kable(corr_tbl |> select(variable, spearman_rho, p_value_label), digits = 3)
variable spearman_rho p_value_label
total_premium 0.205 <2e-16
vehicle_value 0.070 <2e-16
power_to_weight_ratio -0.035 <2e-16
vehicle_age -0.029 <2e-16
driver_age -0.025 <2e-16
seats 0.017 <2e-16
age_driving_licence 0.001 0.703

Draft interpretation to customise: Most group-difference tests are statistically significant because the dataset is large. Practical significance should therefore be judged using effect size, exposure, loss ratio, and business interpretability. The Spearman correlations are statistically significant for several numerical variables, but most coefficients are small; total premium has the strongest monotonic relationship with capped loss ratio among the tested numerical fields.

5 Key analytical findings to review

  1. The portfolio is highly zero-inflated in claims and incurred losses, producing strongly right-skewed loss ratios.
  2. Aggregate loss ratio rises in 2024, suggesting worsening profitability relative to premium.
  3. Policy type is a strong segmentation variable: comprehensive covers, especially COMP_N, have higher aggregate loss ratios.
  4. Bonus score, fuel type, and circulation area show statistically significant and practically visible differences in loss ratio.
  5. Brand-level screening identifies candidates for deeper investigation, but exposure size and mix effects must be considered before drawing underwriting conclusions.
